explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The disciples say, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.” John the Baptist is the one who preached in the wilderness (Mark 1:4). The crowd had a whole lineup of guesses, and he's on it.

Close, but Nehemiah never makes the list. He's the man who led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 2:17). The disciples name John the Baptist, Elijah and one of the prophets. I think Nehemiah was off busy with his wall.

Boaz, the man who married Ruth (Ruth 4:13), isn't on this list. The disciples say people name John the Baptist, Elijah or one of the prophets. Boaz had a great story, he just isn't in this one. Nice try, baker.

That's him! Jesus asks, “Who do you say I am?” and Peter is the one who answers. Peter is one of the twelve (Mark 3:16). When the room goes quiet and everybody stares at their shoes, somebody has to talk. Peter does.

Thomas is one of the twelve, so you're in the right group (Mark 3:18). But in this passage, Peter is the one who answers Jesus. Thomas stays quiet here, at least in what Mark tells us. Keep your guess handy for another day, friend.
Andrew is one of the twelve too (Mark 3:18), so good thinking. But this time the text says Peter answered. Andrew doesn't speak up in these verses. Twelve disciples and only one hand goes up, friend.
Right! Peter answers Jesus, “You are the Christ.” The crowd was handing out other names, but Peter gave Him this one. That's a big answer, baker, and he said it straight out.

Jesus does teach His disciples, and right after this He begins to teach them (Mark 8:31). But that's not what Peter says. His words are, “You are the Christ.” Teacher is a fine word, it just didn't come out of Peter's mouth here.

That's what some people were saying. The disciples told Jesus that some said “one of the prophets.” But when Jesus asks them directly, Peter says something different: “You are the Christ.” The crowd's answer and Peter's answer aren't the same batch.

I get why you'd think so. Somebody says something that big, and you want to run tell the whole neighborhood. But the text says the opposite: “Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him.” Mark doesn't say why, so I won't guess.

Yes, friend. After Peter's answer, the text says Jesus “warned them not to tell anyone about Him.” You'd think He'd say "spread the word!" and He says the opposite. The text doesn't give a reason, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: He must suffer and be killed
explanations.explanation: That's right. Jesus says the Son of Man “must suffer many things” and “must be killed.” He says it plain and doesn't dress it up. That's a hard thing to hear, and I think it was hard for the disciples too.

explanations.answer: He must be crowned in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's a nice picture, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He says the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected, and be killed. Nobody in these verses is talking about a crown. Jesus lays out the hard part first.

Rome never comes up in these verses, baker. Jesus is talking about what the Son of Man must go through: suffering, rejection and being killed. No travel plans on this one. This trip isn't about the map.

That's right! Jesus says the Son of Man must be killed “and after three days rise again.” The hard news doesn't have the last word, and Jesus says so in the same breath. Don't skip the end of that sentence, friend.
Hang on, the sentence isn't over yet! Jesus says He “must be killed and after three days rise again.” That last part is right there in the same sentence. Easy to miss when the first half is so heavy.

I see why you'd think so, since Peter took Him aside privately. But Jesus doesn't agree. He turns, looks at His disciples and rebukes Peter: “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.” That's a no, friend.

Yes, friend. Peter began to rebuke Jesus, and Jesus answers by rebuking Peter. He says, “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.” Jesus doesn't go along with what Peter says.

That's it. Jesus says Peter does not have in mind “the things of God, but the things of men.” It's a strong word from Jesus, so I think it stings. One sentence, two sides, and baker, you picked the right side.

The Law doesn't come up in this moment. Jesus says Peter has in mind “the things of men,” not “the things of God.” It's an easy one to guess because the Law sounds so serious. It's just not in the verse.

The temple isn't mentioned in these verses. What Jesus says is that Peter does not have in mind “the things of God, but the things of men.” Careful with this one, baker. The words are men, not temple.
Right. Jesus says, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” Coming after Him means following Him. Simple words, and a big thing to say yes to.

Leading sounds good, since everybody likes the front of the line. But Jesus says the person must “follow Me.” He's the one out front, friend. I've been behind a lot of people in a lot of lines, and following has a lot going for it.

Teaching is a good thing, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He says anyone who wants to come after Him must “follow Me.” He says that to the crowd and to His disciples both. The word is follow, baker.

It sounds like it should be true. Hold on to your life and you keep it, right? But Jesus says the opposite: “…whoever wants to save his life will lose it…” He flips it right over. I think that's why people lean in.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “…whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.” It's backwards from how we'd think, and He says it anyway. Read it twice if you need to, I did.

explanations.answer: Nothing is worth trading your soul for
explanations.explanation: That's the point. Jesus asks, “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?” Two questions, and the whole world isn't a good trade. I think He wants us to sit with that.

explanations.answer: The whole world is worth the risk
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around. Jesus asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul. He asks it as a question, but the way He asks shows what's at stake. Gaining the whole world isn't the win here.

explanations.answer: Hard work can buy your soul back
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything like that here. He asks, “Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?” and He doesn't list any payment that works. Hard work is a good thing, but it's not in these verses.

Right. Jesus says, “If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation…” It's a serious line, and I think it's meant to be. He doesn't say it with a smile, so I'll keep my jokes in the oven.
Afraid is a good guess, since being afraid and being ashamed can feel close together. But Jesus says “ashamed of Me and My words.” The word is ashamed. Hold onto this one, baker.
Tired is a real thing, friend. I've been tired plenty. But that's not what Jesus says here. His word is “ashamed,” and it's a heavy one.

That's right. Jesus says, “…the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.” It's a sober moment, and the verse says it plainly. I'll let Jesus' words stand just as He said them.

The verse says otherwise, friend. Jesus says if anyone is ashamed of Him and His words, “the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.” It's a heavy line. It's good to read it slowly.

explanations.answer: The kingdom of God arrive with power
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “…there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.” He opens with “Truly I tell you,” so He's saying it plainly. The text doesn't say when, and neither will I, friend.

Fire from heaven is a big picture, but Jesus doesn't say it here. He says they will see “the kingdom of God arrive with power.” It's a good guess, since power sounds like fire. The verse just doesn't say it.

Jesus doesn't say anything about walls here. He says some standing there will see “the kingdom of God arrive with power.” Walls are a job for builders, and Jesus is talking about something else. Not this batch, baker.
